paras: The raids on Black churches in Lafayette and Taylor counties, Florida, were attacks by armed white men on church services in July 1895, reported by Rev. W. Gillisle, presiding elder of the Live Oak district of the African Methodist church. Gillisle said crowds broke up his services in both counties and drove him out, and that churches were being raided, congregations dispersed and pastors driven away. No one was reported shot, but the story ran under the headline "A Reign of Terror" as far away as Idaho, Minnesota and Michigan.

Gillisle, whose district took in the two counties, had recently returned from an attempt to fill his preaching appointments there. The dispatch described Lafayette and Taylor as counties where many Black men had been lynched on charges of assaulting white women, with more than a dozen lynchings in Lafayette in recent months.

According to Gillisle, he was preaching to a large congregation in Lafayette County when a crowd of armed white men entered the church and stationed themselves near the pulpit. Their leaders asked him "How long do you expect to remain in the county and live?" and the men began to shoot, sending Gillisle and the congregation out in a panic. He went on to Bramford, ten miles away, making the trip in an hour.

Gillisle then went to Taylor County, west of Lafayette, where about twenty white men came into a service and stationed themselves around him. He kept preaching until the mob put out the lights, and the congregation fled, some being trampled. The dispatch said the mobs appeared to have shot no one, their object seeming to be "to create terror."

Gillisle said Black residents of the two counties were badly frightened and leaving rapidly, many abandoning their property, and that he would not go back to either county. No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response appears in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from white papers and rested on Gillisle's own report. The Southern Christian Advocate of Charleston, a Methodist weekly, listed it on August 1 under Monday, July 22, noting that the counties were "in locality of recent lynchings for assault on women by negroes." The full dispatch, dated Live Oak, July 24, ran in the Cottonwood Report of Idaho on August 2 with the subhead "Negroes Are Roughly Treated by Wh[ites] in Florida."

That dispatch vouched for the preacher's "good reputation" but ended by saying reported assaults on women had embittered whites against Black residents, setting the raids beside the lynchings. A one-sentence version naming "Rev. D. W. Gillisslee" ran without comment among unrelated domestic news in the Kanabec County Times, the Cape Girardeau Democrat and the L'Anse Sentinel on August 2 and 3. No Black-press coverage was found.

framing.detail: The full dispatch, headlined 'A Reign of Terror', calls the preacher 'roughly treated' and of 'good reputation', then closes by saying reported assaults on women had embittered whites against Black residents in the counties where many had been lynched.
Midwestern weeklies ran the one-sentence condensed brief among unrelated domestic news without comment.
The Methodist Episcopal, South weekly reported the complaint and added that the counties were 'in locality of recent lynchings for assault on women by negroes.'

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of one man's name in wire copy; the same person in every version.
A minor discrepancy in when the report was made; neither dates the incidents themselves.
